title: Signals, jobs, and stopping things properly
objective: By the end of this lesson you can stop a process the right way, understand what kill -9 actually costs, and keep long-running work alive after you disconnect.

blocks.text: You already know how to find a process. This lesson is about the other half: telling it what to do. Linux does that with signals — small messages the kernel delivers to a running process. kill is badly named: it sends a signal, and most of those signals are polite requests.

rows: Shut down cleanly — finish writing, close files, exit
Yes, and that is the point
Yes — many services use it exactly for this
The interrupt you send with Ctrl+C

blocks.caption: Sending them
lines: kill 4821            # TERM by default — the polite request
kill -9 4821         # KILL — no cleanup, last resort
pkill -f myscript.sh # match by command line instead of PID
killall nginx        # every process with that name

blocks.title: What kill -9 actually costs
blocks.text: TERM lets a process finish the write it was in the middle of, flush its buffers, and remove its lock files. KILL gives it none of that. Reaching for -9 first is how you get half-written files, stale locks that block the next start, and databases that need recovery on boot. Try TERM, wait a few seconds, and only then escalate.
Jobs: several things at once in one terminal

blocks.caption: Foreground and background
lines: long-task.sh &        # start it in the background
jobs                  # list what this shell started
fg %1                 # bring job 1 back to the foreground
bg %1                 # let a paused job continue in the background
Ctrl+Z                # pause what is in the foreground
Ctrl+C                # send INT to what is in the foreground

blocks.title: Why your job dies when you close the terminal
blocks.text: When your session ends, the shell sends HUP to the jobs it started — hangup, a name inherited from the era of dial-up terminals. That is why a long copy over SSH dies the moment your laptop sleeps.

blocks.caption: Three ways to keep it running
lines: nohup long-task.sh &         # ignore HUP; output goes to nohup.out
tmux                         # a session you can detach from and return to
systemd-run --user long-task.sh   # hand it to the service manager

blocks.text: For anything you will come back to, tmux is worth learning: start it, run your work inside, press Ctrl+B then d to detach, and reconnect later with tmux attach. The work kept running on the server while your connection did not.

blocks.title: Feel the difference between TERM and KILL
steps: Run: sleep 600 & then: ps aux | grep sleep    (find its PID)
Run: kill -9 <that PID>     (forced — note there is no shutdown at all)
Run: nohup sleep 60 &       (start something that survives a hangup)
blocks.expected: A job you start, list, and stop politely; then the same thing removed by force; and finally a process detached from your session. On a real service the difference between the second and the first is whether its files were closed properly.

cheatsheet: kill sends a signal — it is not only about killing
TERM (15) asks to shut down cleanly · KILL (9) removes it with no cleanup
HUP (1) usually means reload configuration without restarting
Try TERM first, wait, then escalate to -9 only if it is stuck
pkill -f matches the command line · killall matches the name
command & backgrounds · jobs lists · fg/bg move it · Ctrl+Z pauses
Closing the terminal sends HUP to its jobs — that is why they die
nohup, tmux, or a service manager keep work alive after you disconnect

checkpoint.prompt: A service is not responding. Which signal do you send first?

choices.A: KILL (9), to be certain it stops
choices.B: TERM (15), so it can close files and release locks before exiting
choices.D: HUP, which always stops a process

checkpoint.explanation: TERM is the request to shut down cleanly. Escalate to KILL only when the process ignores it, because KILL gives no opportunity to finish writes or clean up locks.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a long-running command die when you close the SSH session that started it?

choices.B: The shell sends HUP to its jobs when the session ends
choices.C: Background jobs always have a time limit
choices.D: The file it was writing gets locked

checkpoint.explanation: Hangup is delivered to the jobs of an ending session. nohup, tmux, or handing the work to a service manager are the ways around it.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the realistic risk of routinely using kill -9?

choices.A: It uses more CPU than kill
choices.B: Half-written files, stale lock files, and data that needs recovery — because the process never gets to clean up
choices.D: There is no risk; it is the recommended default

checkpoint.explanation: KILL cannot be caught or handled. Whatever the process was in the middle of stays in the middle of it.
